lesson.scenario: A router computes hash(key) modulo the shard count and migrates changed owners during a three-to-four shard resize.
entities: Carries account42, order9, user8, and cart17
Maps each key to an unsigned integer
Computes hash modulo N under a routing epoch
connections: apply hash mod active shard count

steps.title: Three-shard map routes deterministic hashes
steps.narration: The router hashes account42=14, order9=7, user8=8, and cart17=17 under N=3.
steps.outcome: Every router selects the same owners without a range directory per key.
steps.invariant: The hash function, shard count, and routing epoch must match across routers.

steps.title: Writes land on computed owners
steps.narration: The router stores order9 on S1 and the three remainder-two keys on S2.
steps.outcome: Placement follows the remainder rather than key ranges or load.
steps.invariant: A write has exactly one authoritative remainder owner in epoch 12.

steps.title: Adding a shard changes the modulo map
steps.narration: A planned N=4 map recalculates owners as [2,3,0,1], moving three of the four probe keys.
steps.outcome: Changing N remaps keys even though their hashes are stable.
steps.invariant: Modulo resizing can move roughly (N-1)/N keys and therefore requires an explicit migration phase.

steps.title: Changed keys copy under dual epochs
steps.narration: The controller copies each remapped row to its epoch-13 owner while epoch 12 remains authoritative.
steps.outcome: New owners are populated without exposing a partially migrated map.
steps.invariant: The old epoch remains authoritative until copies and concurrent-write deltas are complete.

steps.title: Epoch 13 becomes authoritative
steps.narration: After checksums and deltas match, routers atomically switch to N=4 and old owners fence moved keys.
action: publish epoch13 N=4 and fence epoch12 moves
steps.outcome: All requests now use the four-way modulo map.
steps.invariant: An atomic epoch cutover prevents two shards from accepting authoritative writes for one key.

production.scenario: A multi-tenant metrics platform hashes tenant IDs to PostgreSQL shards so every write and read for one customer lands on the same database, even under heavy telemetry bursts.
components: Upload metrics batches tagged with tenant 184 from thousands of services
Owns telemetry admission and schema validation
Maps tenant IDs to shard numbers with the current modulo
Stores one slice of tenant metrics under the current shard count
Receives tenants remapped during the next shard-count increase
Resolves which shard owns a tenant before rendering charts
Backfills tenants when the shard count changes from 16 to 32
flows: Application SDKs send metrics with the tenant ID that the storage layer uses as its partition key.
The ingest API asks the router for the current shard owner instead of embedding shard math in every caller.
Under the current modulo, tenant 184 resolves to shard 03 and every metric row for that tenant lands there.
The dashboard path uses the same router so reads and writes agree on the authoritative shard.
The query API can now issue the chart query directly to the same shard that owns the writes.
When the cluster doubles shard count, the rollout job updates the router to a new mapping version.
Because plain hash partitioning remaps many tenants on a shard-count change, the rollout job bulk-copies affected tenants before cutover.
